incident_edges.relationship: Scott's theory of gender is weighed in Canadian debates over discourse, experience and gender history
incident_edges.evidence_note: Valverde's 1990 review essay in Labour/Le Travail, read in full, treats Scott's Gender and the Politics of History (with Riley) as a key work in 'the controversy about discourse theory'. She notes that poststructuralism had a 'bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)' and that 'in Canada' the debate was posed as 'a yes-or-no question'. She concludes that Scott 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow'. Pierson's 1991 essay on Canadian women's history opens on the turn to deconstruction, with Scott's theorising of gender as its most acclaimed example (opening read). Reference lists show Scott cited by Linda Kealey (1992), Pierson (1992) and Parr's 1995 CHR essay on gender history (OpenAlex metadata; texts unread). Limits: the evidence shows engagement and debate, not adoption. Valverde is sympathetic but critical. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a Canadian critique of the linguistic turn, but its treatment of Scott was not checked here. The 1995–96 Left History exchange is title-level and is not evidence that names Scott. PhD context: 64 of 120 Canadian History PhDs citing Scott engage this field (53%, lift 2.12); 39 engage childhood and youth (lift 3.21), and 49 working-class history (lift 1.87).
incident_edges.map_label: Scott's gender theory in Canadian debates

incident_edges.relationship: Answers Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which he read as reducing class and its material relations to discourse (International Labor and Working-Class History forum, 1987); Scott replied that class struggle is produced in discourse, which she defined to include institutions and social practices. Descent into Discourse (1990) was his subsequent book-length intervention
incident_edges.evidence_note: Scott's position in her own words. 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', International Labor and Working-Class History 31 (Spring 1987), pp. 1–13; only p. 1 was read (publisher's preview image): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; theories of language 'offer a way of thinking about how people construct meaning, about how difference (and therefore sexual difference) operates in the construction of meaning'; labour historians' recent articles on 'language' 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"' (p. 1). Palmer's response in the same issue, 'Response to Joan Scott', pp. 14–23; only p. 14 (preview image) and the notes listed by the publisher were read. It opens on the Halifax strikes of August 1842, with Palmer imagining himself at the scene, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism" and aware of the extent to which "our needs are made of words"', thirsting 'for a dialogue with the participants that will both reveal all and deepen the discourse' (p. 14); n. 2 says the quoted phrases come from Stedman Jones's introduction to Languages of Class and from Ignatieff, 'texts that I take to be related to one another'. Scott's 'A Reply to Criticism', ILWCH 32 (Fall 1987), pp. 39–45, read in full, reports and quotes his response: Palmer and Christine Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language," arguing instead that material reality, social experiences, real or concrete events are the stuff of social history' (p. 39); she quotes his 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened' and answers: 'The opposition discourse versus class struggle is one I cannot accept, for class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40). She defines the term at once: 'By discourse I do not mean utterances, or "words" ... but whole ways of thinking, of understanding how the world operates and what one's place is in it. And not only ways of thinking, but ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies, ways of implementing and justifying inequalities, but also of refusing them'; to say that 'the working class family was created within working-class discourse' 'is not to say that "words" alone brought families into being' (p. 40). The reduction-to-discourse objection is therefore Palmer's interpretation of her argument, which she rejected. She says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me, and little of it has to do with either women or gender' (p. 41), that he implies she has deviated from Marx's dialectical and historical materialism, to which she answers that 'there is more to Marx, greater complexity in his materialism, than Palmer's crude invocation of it' (p. 43), and that 'There is no choice, as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender; each is necessarily incomplete without the other' (p. 45). These are Scott's characterisations of his text. The forum had four voices, not two camps. Christine Stansell ('A Response to Joan Scott', pp. 24–29; only p. 24 read, publisher's preview image) called Scott's essay 'a welcome and important attempt to import some of the sophisticated concerns of current literary criticism into labor history' and sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss—or, more properly, our missed opportunity' (p. 24). Anson Rabinbach ('Rationalism and Utopia as Languages of Nature: A Note', pp. 30–36; only p. 30 read) restated with approval her case that Stedman Jones's language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott grouped Palmer with Stansell on 'language' and wrote that Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); she answered Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (p. 42) and Rabinbach's case for rationalism and universalism (p. 44) separately. The rest of Stansell's and Rabinbach's essays was not read. Later readings, labelled as such: Ted McCoy (2021) quotes the response: 'To say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters' (p. 16, emphasis original) and 'Class is indeed a difficult development to grasp precisely because in both its subjective and objective guises it reproduces the social order at the same time as it challenges it. Language and gender figure in this decisively' (p. 22); he reads Palmer as granting that attention to the gendered features of language is 'indisputable'. Descent into Discourse (1990; unread here) carried the dispute into its chapter on gender: Nicholas Rogers (2021) and Chad Pearson (2021) quote it on Scott's appraisal of women in The Making of the English Working Class: in Pearson's quotation it 'thus tilts too problematically toward the determining power of discourse' (p. 85), while Rogers paraphrases it as tilting 'too problematically towards' it, and as quoting Scott's 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 180), the sentence read above in her 1987 reply. The arrow records Palmer's critique and Scott's rejoinder; it does not judge the dispute. Scott's own critique of Thompson's gendered account of class remains on edge_314 (gender → ep_thompson). Revision 1.152 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §§1.1, 1.5): the publisher's page for Descent into Discourse (Temple University Press; read 2026-10-22; the book remains unread) states its thesis — 'Critical theory is no substitute for historical materialism; language is not life'; reliance on poststructuralism 'reifies discourse and sidesteps structures of oppression and resistance'. Two later readers, labelled as such: Eley and Nield (2000, n. 46, read) call the book the reaction to Scott 'represented most viciously', a hostile characterisation recorded here, not adopted; Scott (2000, p. 69, read in full) puns on its title, 'Assent to Discourse'. The three 2021 Dissenting Traditions essays in the source list are later readings, as this note already says. Palmer's part in the debate as a whole is drawn as bryan_d_palmer → languages_of_class.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott recalls first hearing “gender” used in a paper by Davis at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s (2008); her 1986 essay had quoted Davis’s call to study the significance of the sexes
incident_edges.evidence_note: Scott's own acknowledgement, read in full in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (AHR 113:5, 2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, p. 101): "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90). English renderings are atlas translations from Spanish. Scott sets her own limit on the same page: "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras", and names a second, literary source in her Brown colleagues of the early 1980s. The 1986 quotation of Davis (p. 1054, n. 4) is the existing reading behind edge_1029, which records Davis's contribution to gender history as a field; this edge records Scott's acknowledged personal debt, with the 2008 recollection as new evidence. Not a claim that Davis shared Scott's later theoretical position.
incident_edges.map_label: Davis and Scott’s first hearing of gender, 1970s–2008

incident_edges.relationship: Scott draws on psychoanalytic theory, especially the concept of fantasy, to keep gender a critical question: gender as the relation between the normative and the psychic (2008), fantasy as a concept for feminist history (2011), and the productive incommensurability of psychoanalysis and history (2012)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, pp. 108–109): psychoanalytic theory has been useful to her, "no a sus articulaciones conservadoras"; gender is "el estudio de la relación (en torno a la sexualidad) entre lo normativo y lo psíquico, el intento de colectivizar la fantasía". Her 2012 History and Theory abstract (abstract only): psychoanalysis "can force historians to question their certainty about facts, narrative, and cause". Duke's description of The Fantasy of Feminist History (2011; publisher description): she "advocates fantasy as a useful, even necessary, concept for feminist historical analysis". In a 2018 interview she speaks of "a whole psychoanalytic dimension" in Sex and Secularism. Psychoanalysis as a body of theory is the resource; no particular Freud text is claimed. The 2008 reply explains a use of psychoanalysis that "has been useful" to her ("me ha sido útil"); it does not mark a beginning, since the 1986 essay already engaged psychoanalytic theory critically (edge_583, a separate claim about universal sexual antagonism). She still rejects "conservative" psychoanalysis.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott argues that 1970s psychohistory, shaped by American ego-psychology, assumed a compatibility between psychoanalysis and history that undercut their critical interaction, and proposes a productive incommensurability after de Certeau (2012, in her abstract)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Author's abstract only (History and Theory 51:1, 2012, 63–83); the article body is unread. "This was not the case with the movement for psychohistory that began in the 1970s. Then the influence of American ego-psychology on history-writing promoted the idea of compatibility between the two disciplines in ways that undercut the critical possibilities of their interaction." De Certeau supplies "theoretical insight into the uses of incommensurability"; Lyndal Roper's work shows "both its limits and its value". No strand is targeted: the abstract names American ego-psychology, not a particular psychohistorian. Moderate.

incident_edges.relationship: French feminists caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996), and the parity movement’s attempt to “desymbolize” sex in political representation (Parité!, 2005), as Landes and Dean read them
incident_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: both books are unread. Landes (APSR 1997, p. 443 read) quotes Scott (p. 173): "competing feminist visions have taken one side or another of the opposition between the abstract individual (which counts women the same as men) and the individual self-defined through sexual difference (which insists on their radical unlikeness)". Dean (H-France Review 2006, read in full): the book "focuses on the challenge parité poses to French universalism" (p. 149); Scott quoted on the strategy of "desymbolization" (p. 54) and on "the human individual as plural, as a type of two" (p. 61) (Dean, p. 150); Dean's query about Muslim women and lesbians (p. 152). Scott herself links French universalism, feminist movements and the politics of the veil as objects of one question about how sexual difference is conceived (Unanswered Questions, Spanish translation, p. 108).

incident_edges.relationship: The French headscarf ban read as a symptom of republican, colonial and sexual anxieties (The Politics of the Veil, 2007), and a genealogy of secularism contesting the claim that secular societies guarantee gender equality (Sex and Secularism, 2017), in her reviewers’ accounts and her own interview
incident_edges.evidence_note: Mediated for the books, which are unread. Laborde (Books & Ideas, 2008, read in full): "Particularly acute are Scott’s analyses of the re-importation of the civilizing mission in post-colonial France"; the ban "acted as a (literally) hysterical diversion" from problems of "class, race and gender". Whitney (Literary Review of Canada, 2018, read in full): the book's "polemical aim" is "to counter the notion that gender equality is somehow inherent in secular societies", working through oppositions such as "west versus Orient, Christianity versus Islam". Scott in a 2018 interview (read in full): post-colonial studies were "critical of the notion that modernity was the end point of the civilizing process"; she sought "a critique or a genealogy that could expose these contradictions". Criticism carried here, not drawn as a separate arrow: Laborde finds the "normative premises and broader political implications" unclear, "a standard limitation of discourse analysis"; O'Grady (Times Higher Education, 2018), a philosopher, objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards: Scott is "anachronistic, ahistorical and oddly absolutist in demanding from 19th-century Europeans moral attitudes that tally with her own". Laborde's objection concerns normative premises and political implications; O'Grady's concerns anachronism. In the 2018 interview Scott names her own difficulty: "how do I write a critique of secularism without rejecting it". A contribution to postcolonial critique of the civilizing narrative, not membership of a school.
incident_edges.map_label: Veil, secularism and the civilizing claim, 2007–2017

incident_edges.relationship: Laura Lee Downs charges that Scott’s poststructuralist gender severs experience and subjectivity from the agency of the oppressed and treats discourse as “text-writ-large”; Scott replies that Downs misreads theory, which “analyzes how knowledge is produced” (1993)
incident_edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from women's history, whose experience-and-agency tradition Downs defends. Downs (CSSH 35:2, 1993; p. 414 and the notes shown by the publisher read): Scott's book "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought"; "There is much to admire"; but it contains "a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history"; notes: "Scott treats discourse as text-writ-large". Scott's reply in the same issue (p. 438 read): "profound misapprehension"; "theory analyzes how knowledge is produced; theory does not produce either real life or practical politics." Distinct from Palmer (edge_920), Valverde (edge_967) and Canning (edge_702).

incident_edges.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that they want class 'as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory', and that insisting on class forecloses other political categories: her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (2000)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Body read in full for revision 1.152 (ILWCH 57, 2000, pp. 69–75; Cambridge PDF; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §6.3); the abstract read for 1.147 is confirmed verbatim. Eley and Nield's essay 'will surely become an indispensable assignment in introductory graduate courses because it is synthetic in many senses' (p. 69); they 'are willing to accommodate all manner of deviations from the materialist analyses … especially what some have dubbed "the linguistic turn"', so that one 'might have punned wildly and titled the Eley/Nield essay, "Assent to Discourse"' (p. 69); 'Patrick Joyce has been expelled from the fold and Kathleen Canning is now at its center' (p. 69); 'there's a tension between Eley and Nield's desires to update the old social history by detaching it from its materialist assumptions, on the one hand, and to keep writing narratives of worker political agency, on the other' (pp. 69–70); they talk of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70); Rancière's 1983 essay is 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield' (pp. 70–71); 'They want to define class as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory. To posit them as contradictory is to misunderstand Foucault's ideas about discourse'; 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield's reply (pp. 81–86 read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history' (p. 83), while they 'wholeheartedly applaud Scott's citation of Rancière' (p. 84). Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay) and from languages_of_class → social, which carries the debate's bearing on the field. Earlier note (1.147): Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay).

incident_edges.relationship: With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder, a call for “critical history” as “theorized history”, against a discipline founded on empiricism, “fetishism of archives” and a gendered dismissal of theory (Theses on Theory and History, 2018)
incident_edges.evidence_note: The collective's own words, read in full (English booklet on the History and Theory site, 2018; cited by thesis). Prologue: theory "displaced by empires of empiricism, fetishism of archives, dictates of discipline, enforcement of orthodoxy, and impotent story-telling"; I.1: "Academic history has never managed to transcend its eighteenth century origins as an empiricist enterprise"; II.1: "An invidious distinction between a feminized philosophy and a masculinized history"; III.1: "Critical history is theorized history"; III.7: "Critical history is a history of the present". Co-authored: credit belongs to all three, and no thesis is assigned to Scott alone. A late intervention in disputes about disciplinary scrutiny, not a resolution of them.

incident_edges.relationship: Opened the North American round (ILWCH 1987) by asking labour historians to take language and gender seriously, replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse' (1987), and answered the retrospective with 'The "Class" We Have Lost' (2000): questions that 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either'
incident_edges.evidence_note: 1987, p. 1 (existing reading): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; labour historians 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"'. Reply, ILWCH 32, pp. 40–45 (existing reading, read in full): 'class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it'. 2000, pp. 69–72 (read in full for 1.152): 'Assent to Discourse' (p. 69); 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield (2000, p. 4): 'it was not really until 1987, with Joan Scott's scholarly controversy … that gender concerns … entered the field of vision' of the journal. Her critique of Stedman Jones is drawn separately; her critique of Eley and Nield stays on edge_1127.

incident_edges.relationship: Named critics within the debate beyond Palmer and Valverde, whose arrows exist: Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (1987); Sangster's objection to 'the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (2000); Eley and Nield's charge of an 'ungenerous critique' that allows 'either discourse … or materialist social history' (2000)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Scott's reply (ILWCH 32, p. 42, existing reading) reports Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject'; Stansell's own p. 24 (existing reading) sides with Scott on poststructuralism while holding that social analysis of real women's activities is needed (editors' remarks, read). Sangster 2000 (read in full), pp. 157–158: the Canadian feminists kept 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy', 'unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157; her 'constructed as material' objection on the same page is aimed at Sewell, in Berlanstein's volume, not at Scott); 'The post-structuralist subject thus stands in direct contrast to the Thompsonian subject'. Eley and Nield's reply (2000, p. 83, read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history'. Palmer's critique stays on edge_920 and Valverde's on edge_967; Downs (1993) is named in Scott's entry and not read here.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott faults 'Rethinking Chartism' for using theories of language 'in an essentially conservative manner': treating language as a vehicle for ideas rather than a system of meaning, and so missing the gendered construction of class (1987, as quoted in the ILWCH editors' remarks)
incident_edges.evidence_note: ILWCH 31 'Editor's Remarks', pp. v–vi, read in full (open PDF): Scott 'criticizes Gareth Stedman Jones for using theories of language in his "Rethinking Chartism" in an essentially conservative manner'; he 'stops short of opening up … important conceptual questions' because he treats language as a vehicle for communicating ideas rather than as a system of meaning (p. v, the editors quoting her); her rereading of Chartism finds that its linguistic construction of class meant the working class would be represented by men (pp. v–vi). Scott's own pages are unread beyond p. 1 (existing record); her n. 3 cites Languages of Class. Eley and Nield (2000, p. 7, read): 'Prying open Stedman Jones's exegesis, and breaking its silences over gender', and n. 20: his 'only direct rejoinder to Scott', in the 1997 Lüdtke volume (unread), 'grudgingly admits' her point. Evidence standing: editors' summary and a later reader; Scott's text unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Sangster contrasts Canadian feminist materialist work with what she calls Scott’s more radical antimaterialist deconstruction (2000).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The wording is Sangster’s characterization. Her neighbouring objection about constructed materiality targets Sewell, not Scott.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott explicitly takes de Certeau’s incommensurability as a theoretical resource for a critical relationship between psychoanalysis and history (2012).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The author’s abstract expressly names de Certeau’s theoretical contribution and distinguishes it from Lyndal Roper’s demonstration of limits and value. Abstract read through PubMed PMID 22413176; the article body and de Certeau’s complete works are not newly read.
